text: THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data This chapter records the earlier HLL baseline. A newer lightweight verification compares three grids at the same initial and boundary conditions with a stored finite-grid reference from a separate implementation, including reference-grid sensitivity and unresolved near-wall structure. Open the additional execution and verification Double Mach Reflection This exhibit computes a Mach-10 shock reflecting from a wall using the two-dimensional ideal-gas Euler equations. The benchmark is associated with Woodward and Colella (1984). NASA’s LAVA tutorial is a modern implementation reference. Equations and initial states# Use gamma = 1.4 on [0,4] × [0,1], with conserved state U = (rho, rho u, rho v, E) and E = p/(gamma−1) + rho(u²+v²)/2. The initial shock intersects the bottom wall at x = 1/6 and makes a 60-degree angle with it: xs(y,0)=16+y3.xs​(y,0)=61​+3​y​. The post-shock state to its left is (rho,u,v,p) = (8, 8.25 sqrt(3)/2, −4.125, 116.5). The ambient state to its right is (1.4,0,0,1). The upstream sound speed is one, so the shock-normal propagation speed of ten corresponds to Mach 10. Initial cell states are assigned by the cell-center side of the shock; cut-cell averages are not integrated exactly. The moving incident-shock line is xs(y,t)=16+y+20t3.xs​(y,t)=61​+3​y+20t​. These states satisfy the moving Rankine–Hugoniot relation in the shock-normal direction; the automated check uses normal (sqrt(3)/2,−1/2) and speed 10. Boundary conditions and discretization# The left boundary supplies the post-shock state. The right boundary uses zero-gradient outflow. At the bottom, x < 1/6 supplies post-shock data; the remaining wall reflects normal momentum. The top boundary assigns the two states using x_s(1,t). SSPRK2 stages evaluate this boundary at their corresponding stage times. The calculation uses piecewise-constant finite volumes, a two-wave HLL flux with Davis-type minimum/maximum acoustic speeds, and an unsplit flux divergence. The step is bounded by Δt=C[max⁡(∣u∣+c)Δx+max⁡(∣v∣+c)Δy]−1.Δt=C[Δxmax(∣u∣+c)​+Δymax(∣v∣+c)​]−1. The displayed run has Nx = 256, Ny = 64, delta x = delta y = 1/64, C = 0.4, final time 0.2, and 811 steps. Its minimum final density is 1.4 and minimum final pressure is 1.0. These are measured diagnostics for this run, not a general positivity theorem. Reproduce and inspect# python -m numart.cli run double-mach --n 64 --cfl 0.4 --output outputs/double-mach Here --n sets Ny and Nx = 4 Ny. The command saves solution.npz, run.json, and double-mach.png. The gallery snapshot includes its run manifest and conserved-state arrays. Array q has shape (Nx,Ny,4); x and y are cell-center coordinates. The manifest records source hashes and the working-tree state at generation time. What the figure establishes# The image shows a computed incident/reflected shock pattern, with density and thirty density contours. First-order spatial reconstruction is deliberately diffusive. This grid does not resolve the fine wall jet and roll-up of high-resolution PPM or adaptive calculations. There is no exact final-time solution, grid-convergence study, or digitized original-paper comparison in this exhibit. Tests check equal-state flux consistency, a periodic uniform state, the incident-shock jump relation, moving-top and reflecting-wall data, and admissible states in a small-grid run. They do not establish convergence of the full reflection pattern. Further work should add higher-order reconstruction, refinement, and independent reference-code comparisons. For strong-shock instability diagnostics, continue to the carbuncle phenomenon. This HLL image is not a demonstration that a Roe implementation is stable or unstable. Watch the reflection evolve# The saved-state movie shows density and pressure from the same 256 × 64 calculation.
